# Why CNNs Work for Images


## Properties of Image Data

![Three regions (sky, cow, grass) at three scales: 12, 48 and 192 pixels. [Image Source](https://unsplash.com/de/fotos/braune-schafe-auf-grunem-grasfeld-tagsuber-olonUwUrmQk)]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cows2_multiscale.png){width=100%}

::: {.incremental}
- **High-Dimensional**: An RGB image of size $224 \times 224$ has $224 \times 224 \times 3 = 150{,}528$ values
- **Locality**: Nearby pixels are statistically related (edges, textures, objects)
- **Stability under transformations**: A cow should be recognized regardless of position
- **Hierarchical Structure**: Features at multiple scales (pixels → edges → textures → objects)
:::


## MLPs Need Flat Inputs

::: {#fig-cnn-mlp}
![ ]({{< meta params.images_path >}}mlp_images_example.png)

Image $\in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ → flatten → vector $\in \mathbb{R}^p$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Flattening **destroys spatial structure**.
:::

## MLPs and How they Learn

![]({{< meta params.images_path >}}mlp_images_examples_permutation.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.fragment}
**Question**: Can an MLP learn from images whose pixels are shuffled with a fixed permutation $\m{P}$, i.e. $f(\m{P}\vect{x})$?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Yes, equally well: an MLP does not use the **neighbourhood** of pixels. We need an architecture with **inductive biases** for images.
:::


## Invariance and Equivariance

::: {.fragment}
**Invariant** — output unchanged by transformation:
$$f(g(\vect{x})) = f(\vect{x})$$
*"I don't care about the transformation."*
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Equivariant** — output transforms with input:
$$f(g(\vect{x})) = g(f(\vect{x}))$$
*"I transform my output the same way."*
:::

# How CNNs Work

## History: Experiments on Cats

::: {#fig-cnns-huber-wiesel}

![Illustration [Source](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-28954-6_4/figures/1)]({{< meta params.images_path >}}huber_wiesel_cat_experiment.jpg)

:::


## The CNN Idea

::: {#fig-cnn-cnn-spatial}
![Source: @johnson_eecs_2019]({{< meta params.images_path >}}cnn_spatial.jpg){width=25%}

A neuron only connects to a small spatial patch of the input.
:::

::: {.incremental}
1. **Local connectivity**: a neuron sees a small spatial region
2. **Parameter sharing**: the same filter at every position
3. **Translation equivariance**: input shifts → output shifts
:::


## Inductive Bias

::: {.incremental}
- MLPs:  minimal bias, very general, **data-hungry**
- CNNs:  assume **locality + translation equivariance**
- Transformers:  assume **long-range dependencies**
:::

::: {.fragment}
Choosing an architecture = choosing which assumptions to bake in.
:::



## Convolution on RGB Images

::: {#fig-cnns-intro-example}

![Source:  @prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}convolution_prince_rgb.png)

:::

::: {.fragment}
\begin{equation}
S(i, j) = (K * I)(i, j) = \sum_m \sum_n I(i + m, j + n) K(m, n) + b
\end{equation}

$I$: input, $K$: kernel (smaller than $I$), $b$: bias
:::

# Part 2: Filters, Feature Maps, and Hierarchies


## Convolution Hyperparameters

Key parameters to configure a convolutional layer:

::: {.incremental}
- **Kernel Size** ($k$): Spatial extent (typically $3\times3$ or $5\times5$)
- **Padding** ($p$): Zero-padding added to input borders
- **Stride** ($s$): Step size when moving the kernel
- **Dilation** ($d$): Spacing between kernel elements
:::


## Demo: Convolution Parameters

<div style="height: 835px;">
<iframe data-src="../../demos/cnns/convolution_parameters/index.html" width="1460" height="705" style="border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 6px; transform: scale(1.18); transform-origin: top left;" title="Interactive demo: kernel size, padding, stride and dilation of a convolution"></iframe>
</div>

Task "Reduce the resolution": 3 × 3 kernel, output 5 × 5. [Open in new tab](../../demos/cnns/convolution_parameters/index.html){target="_blank"}


## Formulas

Output size ($i$: input size, $k$: kernel, $p$: padding, $s$: stride, $d$: dilation):

\begin{equation}
o = \left\lfloor \frac{i + 2p - d\cdot(k-1) - 1}{s} + 1 \right\rfloor
\end{equation}

::: {.fragment}
Number of parameters ($C_{in}$ input channels, $C_{out}$ filters, one bias per filter):

\begin{equation}
\text{Total Parameters} = (k \times k \times C_{in} \times C_{out}) + C_{out}
\end{equation}
:::


## Quiz: Output Shape & Parameters

- Input: $3 \times 32 \times 32$ (C, H, W)
- Convolution: 10 filters, kernel $5 \times 5$, stride=1, pad=2

**1.** Output size? **2.** Number of parameters?

::: {.fragment}
**1.** $o = \lfloor \frac{32 + 4 - 4 - 1}{1} + 1 \rfloor = 32$ → output $10 \times 32 \times 32$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**2.** $(5 \times 5 \times 3 \times 10) + 10 = 760$ parameters
:::

::: {.fragment}
Padding 2 preserves the spatial size with kernel 5.
:::

## Receptive Field: Formula

The receptive field of a CNN $r_0$:

\begin{equation}
r_0 = \sum_{l=1}^L \left( (k_l - 1) \prod_{i=1}^{l-1} s_i \right) + 1
\end{equation}

- $L$: Total number of layers
- $k_l$: Kernel size at layer $l$
- $s_i$: Stride at layer $i$, from layer 1 up to $l-1$


## Quiz: Receptive Field

Three layers, each $k = 3$, $s = 1$. What is the receptive field $r_0$?

::: {.fragment}
$$r_0 = (3-1) + (3-1) + (3-1) + 1 = 7$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Three $3\times3$ convs see $7\times7$, with $3 \times 9 = 27$ weights instead of $49$ for one $7\times7$ (per channel pair).
:::

# More Layers & Operations

## Downsampling

Spatial downsampling reduces resolution (H×W → H'×W'): stride $> 1$ (learned) or pooling (fixed).

![a) Sub-Sampling, b) Max Pooling, c) Average Pooling. Source: @prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}downsampling_with_pooling.jpg){width=80%}


## Upsampling

Needed when the output must have pixel resolution, e.g. **segmentation**.

![a) Duplicate, b) Max-Unpooling, c) Bilinear Interpolation. Source: @prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}upsampling_options.jpg){width=80%}

::: {.fragment}
Also: **transposed convolutions** (learnable upsampling).
:::


## 1×1 Convolutions

$(C_{in} \times H \times W) \rightarrow (C_{out} \times H \times W)$: change the number of channels, no spatial mixing.

::: {#fig-cnn-1x1}

![Source: @prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}1x1_conv_example.jpg)

:::


## Global Average Pooling

Averages each activation map: $(C \times H \times W) \rightarrow (C \times 1 \times 1)$. Often used right before the classifier.

::: {#fig-cnn-global-avg-pooling}

![Global Average pooling, input (left) and output (right).]({{< meta params.images_path >}}global_average_pooling.jpg)
:::


## Quiz: MLP vs CNN Efficiency

**CIFAR-10 Images**: $32 \times 32 \times 3$

::: {.fragment}
**MLP**: 2 hidden layers (256, 128 neurons)

How many parameters in first layer?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**CNN**: 2 conv layers (16 filters, $3\times3$, then 32 filters, $3\times3$)

How many parameters in first layer?
:::

## Quiz: Solutions

::: {.fragment}
**MLP first layer:**

$(32 \times 32 \times 3) \times 256 = 3{,}072 \times 256 = 786{,}432$ parameters
:::

::: {.fragment}
**CNN first layer:**

$(3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 16) + 16 = 432 + 16 = 448$ parameters
:::

::: {.fragment}
**CNN uses 1,755× fewer parameters!** 🚀
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Why?** Local connectivity + parameter sharing = massive efficiency!
:::
